transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Could you start by telling me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I guess I'm here because things have been getting really complicated at work lately. I'm a transportation inspector for the county, you know, checking the buses, the maintenance yards, making sure everything is up to code. And I've always done a good job. A really good job, actually. In fact, just a few months ago, I won this county safety award. It was a big deal, a plaque, a little ceremony, the whole nine yards. I thought it was a good thing, you know? Recognition for all the extra hours I put in, making sure no one cuts corners. 

But ever since that award... things have changed. It's like it put a target on my back. Certain people—and I won't name names just yet, but people I work with every single day—they've started twisting my inspection reports. I write down a minor infraction, something standard, and suddenly it's being blown out of proportion, or worse, they're acting like I missed something huge. And then come the questions. Pointed questions about the budget, about how much time I'm spending at certain sites, like they're trying to imply I'm doing something shady, like I'm crooked or taking kickbacks or something. 

I tried to talk to my supervisor about it. I sat down with him last Tuesday—no, Wednesday—and I laid it all out. I showed him the discrepancies. And he just brushed it off. He told me it's just a "normal review process," that everyone gets scrutinized. But I know what normal looks like. I've been doing this for years. This isn't normal. I can tell, I can just feel it, there is a coordinated effort going on behind the scenes to completely discredit me. They want me out, Doctor. They want to ruin my reputation, and I just... I don't know who to trust anymore.
Can you tell me exactly how long you've been feeling that your coworkers are deliberately trying to discredit you—has this been going on for weeks, or longer than that?

Weeks? No, no, Dr. Smith, it’s been way longer than a few weeks. If I really sit down and map out the timeline—which I have, actually, I’ve kept track of when the shift in their behavior started—it’s been going on for about a year now. A full twelve months. 

It traces back exactly to when I got recognized for that county safety initiative. I mean, before that, I was just another guy in the fleet yard, right? Just doing my job, checking the brake lines, filing the standard forms, keeping my head down. But that initiative... I had spent all this extra time putting together a completely new checklist for the hazardous materials transport, just trying to make sure we didn't have any spills or liability issues for the county. And the upper management, the brass, they loved it. They made a really big show of it. 

But almost the very next day—literally, I remember it was a Tuesday, right after the Monday morning all-hands meeting—the atmosphere in the office just... soured. It was palpable. So for a whole year, I’ve had to sit there and watch them slowly escalate this. First it was just passive-aggressive stuff, you know, suddenly my files would get "misplaced" on someone else's desk, or I'd get left off important emails about schedule changes. But over the last twelve months, it’s turned into this deliberate, calculated campaign to make me look incompetent. Every single month they add a new layer to it. So yeah, it hasn't been weeks. It's been a year. A very long, exhausting year of constantly having to defend every single mark I make on a clipboard.
Aside from these suspicions about your coworkers, have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that others around you didn't seem to hear or see?

Voices? Like... like you think I'm crazy? No, no, Dr. Smith, absolutely not. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. My hearing is actually perfect. It has to be for my job, you know? When you're out in the maintenance yard, you have to be able to hear the hiss of a tiny air brake leak from fifty yards away, and you have to be able to pick that sound out over the noise of three idling diesel engines. I get my hearing and vision checked every two years for the county physical, and I always pass with flying colors. 20/20 vision, perfect hearing. 

So, no, I'm not... I'm not imagining things. I know exactly what's real. And honestly, that's what makes this whole situation at work so incredibly frustrating. If I were just making things up in my head, if I were seeing shadows or hearing ghosts or something, it would almost be easier, wouldn't it? Because then the problem would just be me, and I could just take a pill or something and it would go away. But I'm not. The things I'm seeing are real ink on real paper, real emails being routed around me, real whispers when I walk into the breakroom. 

I mean, I hear them talking, sure, but they're real coworkers actually talking about me right there in the room, not voices inside my brain. I'm completely grounded in reality here, Doctor. I don't see visions. I just pay very, very close attention to my actual, physical surroundings, which is exactly why I've been able to piece together what they're doing to me over this past year. You have to be observant in my line of work, and I just apply that same observation to the office. So no, no voices. Just real people causing real problems for me.

Outside of this situation at work, do you also find yourself distrustful or suspicious of people close to you, like family members or friends, or has this feeling of being targeted been limited specifically to your coworkers over this past year?

No, no, it's just work. Just them. My family... my family is fine. Well, I mean, my mom calls me every Sunday, like clockwork, right around 4:00 PM, usually right after she finishes watching her afternoon shows, and she asks about everything, and I tell her about work, and she's always been supportive. She doesn't understand the technical side of the inspections, obviously, she doesn't know a brake shoe from a steering column, but she listens. And my brother, he lives out in Denver, he's a software engineer, totally different field, but we text a few times a week about football, about the Broncos, mostly. He's a huge fan, I'm more of a casual watcher, but it's a good connection. I trust them completely. I would never, ever suspect them of anything. 

And my friends, too. I've got a solid group of guys I play softball with on Thursday nights during the summer. We've been playing together since high school. We go to O'Malley's after the games, grab a few pitchers, talk about life. I trust those guys with my life. If one of them needed help moving a couch at 2:00 AM, I'd be there, and they'd do the same for me. There's no hidden agenda with them. We just play ball and drink beer. 

So, no, it's really, specifically, entirely isolated to the people at the county office. It's the people who have access to my reports, the people who stand to benefit if I get pushed out or if my credibility is ruined. Because if I'm gone, they can go back to being lazy, they can go back to pencil-whipping the inspection forms instead of actually doing the work. My family and friends don't care about county transport protocols. It's just my coworkers. It's a very specific, localized threat, Dr. Smith. I'm not some paranoid guy who thinks the whole world is out to get him. I just know exactly who is out to get me at work, and I can prove it if anyone would just look at the paperwork properly instead of covering for them.

Before this situation started about a year ago, would you say you were generally a trusting person, or have you always tended to be wary and suspicious of other people's motives, even back in your teens or early twenties?

Trusting? Yeah, I'd say I was. I mean, I wasn't naive, right? I didn't just hand over my wallet to a stranger on the street, but I wasn't... I wasn't like this. If you look back at my teens, like when I was in high school—I went to Westside High, graduated in 2014—I was just a regular guy. I played baseball, I hung out with my friends, I assumed people generally meant what they said. I remember this one time, my senior year, I lent my car—it was this beat-up old Honda Civic, barely ran, but it was mine—I lent it to a buddy of mine, Dave, so he could take his girlfriend to prom because his car was in the shop. I didn't even think twice about it. I just handed him the keys. I trusted him completely. And he brought it back, full tank of gas, no problems. That's how I operated. 

Even in my early twenties, when I first started working for the county, right out of school. I started as a junior mechanic, just doing oil changes and rotating tires on the county fleet vehicles. I trusted my supervisor, Mr. Henderson. Good guy. He taught me a lot about diesel engines. I trusted the guys I worked with. We'd share tools, we'd cover for each other if someone was running five minutes late. There was no... no malice, you know? No hidden agendas. I just assumed that if you did a good job, people respected you for it. I thought that was the deal. You work hard, you follow the rules, and people treat you fairly. 

So, no, I haven't always been wary. I haven't always been looking over my shoulder. This whole thing, this hyper-awareness, this constant need to double-check every single interaction... it's exhausting, Dr. Smith. It really is. It's not who I am by nature. It's who I've had to become because of what they're doing. If they hadn't started this campaign against me a year ago, if they had just let me do my job and be recognized for that safety initiative, I'd still be that same trusting guy. But they changed the rules of the game, and I had to adapt just to survive in that office. I didn't ask for this. I really didn't. I just wanted to make sure the hazardous materials were transported safely. That's all I wanted.

Functioning outside the delusional system (family relationships, friendships, occupational competence aside from the perceived conspiracy) is well preserved, and the delusion is encapsulated to a specific, circumscribed theme (workplace persecution) rather than bizarre or diffuse. This pattern—non-bizarre, circumscribed delusion(s) lasting >1 month without other psychotic symptoms and without significant functional deterioration—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional symptoms/functional decline) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (no depressive/manic episode elicited).
